quirk_lead.text: Its 1992 Detroit Auto Show unveiling reportedly involved driving the new Jeep through a plate-glass window with Chrysler's chairman aboard
quirk_lead.note: Research lead only -- not a verified fact. Must not be assumed as the thesis until supported by claims in this fact pack. RESEARCH FINDING: this lead was specifically wrong -- no chairman was in the vehicle; see reveal02/reveal03.

claims.normalized_claim: No Jeep Grand Cherokee existed in 1990. The nameplate was first shown to the public on January 7, 1992 and went on sale for the 1993 model year.

sources.title: Jeep Grand Cherokee (ZJ)
sources.evidence_note: States the ZJ was introduced at the 1992 Detroit auto show for model year 1993; no earlier model year is listed.

claims.safe_wording: There was no Grand Cherokee in 1990 -- the nameplate didn't exist yet. It debuted in January 1992, for the 1993 model year.
forbidden_or_unsupported_inference: That a 1990 Grand Cherokee model exists and this pack is simply about an early example of it
claims.notes: The episode brief's topic string specifies '1990'; this is the single most important finding of A-PRE research and must be addressed head-on in the episode rather than silently corrected. See open_questions in producer_outline.

claims.normalized_claim: Development of what became the Grand Cherokee began under American Motors Corporation (AMC) around 1985, as a planned successor to the compact Jeep Cherokee (XJ) and the aging full-size Wagoneer (SJ). Chrysler acquired AMC in 1987 and continued the program through to its 1992 launch -- a development period of roughly seven years.

sources.title: Jeep Grand Cherokee (ZJ)
sources.evidence_note: Describes AMC-era origin, 1987 Chrysler acquisition, and continuation of the program.

sources.title: The 1993 Jeep Grand Cherokee Was a Game-Changer
sources.evidence_note: Independently characterizes the ZJ as '7+ years in the making,' corroborating the AMC-era start date.

claims.safe_wording: The project actually started under American Motors, years before Chrysler owned Jeep at all -- Chrysler bought AMC in 1987 and inherited a program already underway.
forbidden_or_unsupported_inference: That Chrysler conceived the Grand Cherokee from scratch

claims.normalized_claim: Stylist Larry Shinoda produced an early prototype design for the Grand Cherokee in 1985. AMC initially claimed the design as its own work, which led to litigation; after Chrysler's acquisition of AMC, Chrysler settled with Shinoda's estate for more than $200,000.

sources.title: Jeep Grand Cherokee (ZJ)
sources.evidence_note: Only source found describing the Shinoda design-credit dispute and settlement amount.

claims.safe_wording: According to Wikipedia's account, designer Larry Shinoda's 1985 prototype touched off a design-credit dispute that Chrysler eventually settled with his estate for over $200,000.
forbidden_or_unsupported_inference: That the dispute was resolved in court rather than by settlement
That Shinoda's design is exactly what reached production unmodified
claims.notes: Reputation-sensitive claim (legal dispute) resting on a single reference source -- did not find independent corroboration within the research budget for this test run. Kept airable but hedged with clear attribution rather than stated as flat fact.

claims.normalized_claim: The Grand Cherokee debuted publicly on January 7, 1992 at the North American International Auto Show in Detroit (Cobo Hall), ahead of 1993 model year sales.

sources.title: Jeep Grand Cherokee (ZJ)
sources.evidence_note: Confirms January 1992 introduction date at Detroit auto show.

sources.title: Jeep Celebrates Past, Looks to Electrified Future at Detroit Auto Show
sources.evidence_note: Independently places the debut at the 1992 Detroit show at Cobo Hall.

claims.safe_wording: It was unveiled on January 7, 1992, at the Detroit auto show, months before the 1993 models reached showrooms.

claims.normalized_claim: At the Cobo Hall unveiling, a Chrysler executive drove a Grand Cherokee up a flight of steps and through a plate-glass window, having driven it from the Jefferson North Assembly Plant with Detroit Mayor Coleman Young riding along and a police escort; the glass was fake theatrical 'sugar glass' rather than real glazing.

sources.title: Jeep Grand Cherokee (ZJ)
sources.evidence_note: Names the executive, Mayor Coleman Young as passenger, the Jefferson North starting point, and Cobo Hall as the venue.

sources.title: Jeep Grand Cherokee
sources.evidence_note: Independently corroborates the stunt and adds that the shattered glass was fake 'sugar glass' used for stage effects.

claims.safe_wording: A Chrysler executive drove a Grand Cherokee up the steps of Cobo Hall and straight through a plate-glass window -- with Detroit's mayor riding along and a police escort the whole way. The glass shattering was a stage trick, not real glazing.
forbidden_or_unsupported_inference: That the stunt used real glass or put anyone at genuine risk
That the driver was Chrysler's chairman/CEO -- see reveal03 for who it actually was
claims.notes: This corrects the episode_brief's seeded quirk_lead, which assumed 'Chrysler's chairman' was aboard -- research shows the driver was Chrysler's president (Bob Lutz, see reveal03), not the chairman, and the passenger was Detroit's mayor, not a Chrysler executive at all.

claims.normalized_claim: The executive who drove through the window was Bob Lutz, who held the title of Chrysler President at the time (Lee Iacocca remained Chrysler's Chairman/CEO until Robert Eaton succeeded him on January 1, 1993).

sources.title: Bob Lutz (businessman)
sources.evidence_note: Career timeline places Lutz as Chrysler president in this period, before his later vice-chairman role.

sources.title: So Long, Bob. Hello Bob: Chrysler's Lutz isn't ready to settle down
sources.evidence_note: Confirms Lutz remained Chrysler president through the Eaton transition on January 1, 1993, i.e. was president, not CEO, in January 1992.

claims.safe_wording: That driver was Bob Lutz, Chrysler's president at the time -- not the company's chairman, who was still Lee Iacocca.
forbidden_or_unsupported_inference: That Iacocca personally drove or rode in the stunt vehicle
conflicting_evidence: One search-engine synthesis of the Wikipedia ZJ article's content labeled Lutz 'CEO' at the time of the stunt; that label conflicts with Lutz's own career timeline (Wikipedia bio) and a WardsAuto retrospective, both of which place him as president in this period with Iacocca still chairman/CEO. Titled him 'president' here as the better-corroborated reading.
claims.notes: Kept at medium rather than high because the two supporting sources are both search-snippet-only, and one competing summary used a different title -- exactly the kind of role/title detail that's easy to blur.

claims.normalized_claim: One source states that Lee Iacocca personally delayed the Grand Cherokee's release until late 1992.

sources.title: Jeep's Original Grand Cherokee Tackled Country Roads and Country Clubs
sources.evidence_note: Direct fetch returned HTTP 403; this claim is only known via an aggregated search-engine synthesis, not from reading the article itself.

claims.safe_wording: Unresolved -- do not assert. If mentioned at all, frame only as 'according to one account' with no causal claim about why the timing happened.
forbidden_or_unsupported_inference: That Iacocca masterminded the launch timing
That Iacocca was personally involved in the plate-glass stunt itself
conflicting_evidence: Not mentioned in the more detailed Wikipedia AMC/Chrysler development-timeline account, which attributes the multi-year delay to the AMC-to-Chrysler transition generally rather than to an Iacocca decision specifically.
claims.notes: The source that raised this claim could not be read directly (403) and the claim wasn't independently corroborated within this test run's research budget -- recorded honestly as unresolved rather than dropped silently or guessed at.

claims.normalized_claim: Across its 1993-1998 run the Grand Cherokee (ZJ) offered a 4.0L AMC-designed inline-six (190 hp for 1993-1995, 185 hp for 1996-1998), an optional 5.2L Magnum V8 (225 hp), a 5.9L Magnum V8 (245 hp, 1998 Limited only), and a 2.5L VM Motori diesel four-cylinder for export markets.

sources.title: Jeep Grand Cherokee (ZJ)
sources.evidence_note: Engine table with displacement, horsepower and model-year applicability.

claims.safe_wording: Engines ranged from a 190-horsepower inline-six up to a 245-horsepower V8 in the last model year, plus a diesel option sold only outside the US.
claims.notes: Ordinary spec background -- reference source alone is sufficient per evidence-proportionality guidance.

claims.normalized_claim: The Grand Cherokee launched with a standard driver-side airbag on every model, was positioned as the first mid-size SUV to offer V8 power as an option, and introduced Jeep's Quadra-Trac full-time four-wheel-drive system.

sources.title: Jeep Grand Cherokee (ZJ)
sources.evidence_note: Lists these as notable firsts for the model.

claims.safe_wording: It came with a driver's airbag as standard on every model, was marketed as the first mid-size SUV you could get with a V8, and introduced Jeep's full-time Quadra-Trac 4WD.
forbidden_or_unsupported_inference: That it was the first SUV of any kind or any size with a driver airbag or V8 -- the claim is specific to the mid-size SUV segment
That Quadra-Trac itself was a brand-new Jeep invention rather than a system introduced on this model
claims.notes: 'Firsts' claims are marketing-adjacent and single-sourced -- kept airable but scoped tightly to what the source actually says (segment-specific), not broadened.

claims.normalized_claim: Sources disagree on the exact 1993 Grand Cherokee base MSRP: figures found range from about $18,990 to $21,898 depending on trim and which aggregator is cited, with the Laredo 4-door specifically listed around $19,930.

sources.title: 1993 Jeep Grand Cherokee Specifications
sources.evidence_note: One of several pricing figures found in aggregated search results; did not resolve to one canonical number.

sources.title: The 2024 Jeep Grand Cherokee Is Over $9,000 Cheaper Than A 1993 Model, How Much Better Is It?
sources.evidence_note: Cites the higher-end figure used for its inflation-adjusted comparison.

claims.safe_wording: Depending on trim, it launched at roughly $19,000 to $22,000 -- no single 'the' base price reconciles every source found.
forbidden_or_unsupported_inference: Any single exact price stated without the 'roughly/depending on trim' hedge
conflicting_evidence: $21,898 vs. $18,990 vs. Laredo-specific $19,930 -- not resolved within this test run's research budget; may reflect base 2-door vs. loaded 4-door confusion across aggregator sites rather than a genuine primary-source conflict.
claims.notes: Did not chase a KBB primary figure further -- direct fetch was blocked (403) and this is a background/color number, not the thesis, so proportional effort stops here per the soft research budget.

claims.normalized_claim: Total ZJ-generation production across the 1993-1998 model years was 1,251,473 units.

sources.title: Jeep Grand Cherokee (ZJ)
sources.evidence_note: States total production figure in the infobox/body.

claims.safe_wording: Over its six model years, Jeep built more than 1.25 million of them.
claims.notes: Single-sourced; did not find independent corroboration within this test run's budget. Kept at medium rather than high for that reason alone.

claims.normalized_claim: Of the roughly 1.25 million ZJs built, only 6,378 were the top-spec Grand Wagoneer trim, which was offered solely for the 1993 model year.

sources.title: Jeep Grand Cherokee (ZJ)
sources.evidence_note: States the Grand Wagoneer variant's production count and single-model-year availability.

claims.safe_wording: Only 6,378 were the range-topping Grand Wagoneer trim, and it was gone again after just one model year.

claims.normalized_claim: Beyond the primary Jefferson North Assembly Plant in Detroit, the ZJ was also produced for local/export markets in Graz, Austria (by Magna Steyr), Cordoba, Argentina, and Valencia, Venezuela.
claims.safe_wording: It wasn't just a Detroit product -- it was also assembled in Austria, Argentina, and Venezuela for those local markets.
forbidden_or_unsupported_inference: That non-US plants used identical specification/build to the Detroit-built trucks
claims.notes: Single-sourced background fact, ordinary per evidence-proportionality guidance.

claims.normalized_claim: The Grand Cherokee was positioned as a new, larger model sitting above the compact Jeep Cherokee (XJ), aimed at eventually taking over the role of the aging, truck-based Wagoneer (SJ) lineage -- rather than replacing the Cherokee (XJ) outright, which continued in production alongside it.

sources.title: Jeep Grand Cherokee (ZJ)
sources.evidence_note: Describes the intended relationship to the XJ Cherokee and SJ Wagoneer.

claims.safe_wording: It slotted in above the smaller Cherokee, which kept selling alongside it, effectively taking over the role the old, truck-based Wagoneer had held.
forbidden_or_unsupported_inference: That the compact Cherokee (XJ) was discontinued when the Grand Cherokee arrived -- it was not
